ta-tliltocatl-albopilosus.title: Curly Hair Tarantula
ta-tliltocatl-albopilosus.summary: A fluffy-looking, slow-moving, docile ground tarantula from Central America and a classic beginner species. It likes a deep substrate to dig in, a cork hide and a full water dish.
rows: About 6–6.5 in (15–17 cm) leg span; body about 3 in
Females up to 20–25 years; males about 5 years
Ground-dwelling: wider than tall, with a tight, ventilated lid. Floor at least 3× the leg span (4–5× is better); a 12-in cube suits an adult
Fill about half the enclosure with a burrow-friendly soil mix; add a half cork round as a hide
Moderate: keep the lower substrate damp and the top dry; wet one corner every few weeks
Adults: a few crickets or a roach every 2–3 weeks; remove leftovers within 24 hours. Wait several days after a molt before feeding
Docile and rarely defensive, but it can flick irritating (urticating) hairs; handling is not needed

sources.name: The Tarantula Collective – Tliltocatl albopilosus care guide

ta-theraphosa-blondi.title: Goliath Birdeater Tarantula
ta-theraphosa-blondi.summary: The heaviest spider in the world, from the rainforests of northern South America. It grows fast and big, has some of the most irritating defensive hairs of any tarantula and a painful bite, so it's for experienced keepers.
rows: Leg span up to about 11 in (28 cm); body up to about 4–5 in. Can weigh about 175 g
Females up to about 25 years; males about 5 years
Large ground enclosure, wider than tall, with a tight lid (e.g. 12–18 in cube or larger)
Fill half to two-thirds with a burrow-friendly soil mix; cork hide
Moderate to high: keep lower substrate moist, let the top dry between waterings to prevent mold
Adults: several large crickets or one large roach every 2–3 weeks
Not recommended: very irritating urticating hairs and a painful bite
Northern Brazil, the Guianas and southern Venezuela
warn: Advanced species: strong defensive hairs and a painful bite. Do not handle.

sources.name: The Tarantula Collective – Goliath birdeater care guide

ta-aphonopelma-seemanni.title: Striped Knee Tarantula (Costa Rican Zebra)
ta-aphonopelma-seemanni.summary: A dark tarantula with white stripes at the leg joints from dry forest and scrub in Central America. Calm and inclined to retreat into its burrow, it's a good low-maintenance beginner species.
rows: Leg span about 5–6 in (15 cm); body about 3.5 in
Ground enclosure at least 3× the leg span (4× is better), wider than tall, tight lid
Fill half to two-thirds with soil mix so it can dig; cork hide
Moderate: adults do best with substrate that dries between waterings
Adults: 4–5 adult crickets every 3–4 weeks; skip feeding if the abdomen looks oversized
Calm; more likely to run and hide than to show aggression. Handling is not needed
Western Costa Rica, Honduras, Nicaragua and possibly Guatemala (semi-arid scrub)

sources.name: The Tarantula Collective – Aphonopelma seemanni care guide

ta-lasiodora-parahybana.title: Brazilian Salmon Pink Birdeater Tarantula
ta-lasiodora-parahybana.summary: One of the largest tarantulas in the world, from northeastern Brazil, with salmon-pink hairs on its legs. It grows quickly and is fairly docile, but its size and irritating hairs call for careful handling of the enclosure.
rows: Leg span up to 11 in (28 cm), most 8–9 in; females can top 100 g
Females up to about 15 years; males about 5 years
Ground enclosure at least 3× the leg span (4–5× is better), wider than deep to reduce fall risk
Fill about half with a burrow-friendly soil mix; cork hide
Moderate: lower layers moist, top layers drying between waterings
Adults: 4–5 large crickets or one large roach every 2–3 weeks
Generally docile but has irritating (urticating) hairs; avoid handling
Medium to fast (adult size in about 2 years)

sources.name: The Tarantula Collective – Lasiodora parahybana care guide

ta-cyriopagopus-lividus.title: Cobalt Blue Tarantula
ta-cyriopagopus-lividus.summary: A striking electric-blue burrowing tarantula from Myanmar and Thailand. It spends most of its life underground, is quick and defensive, and has medically significant venom, so it's strictly for advanced keepers.
rows: Leg span about 5 in (13 cm); body about 3.5 in
Deep burrowing enclosure (e.g. an 8–12 in tall cube) with most of the space filled with substrate
Fill at least half to three-quarters with soil mix; it digs deep burrows
Moderate to high: lower substrate damp but never waterlogged
Adults: 4–5 large crickets or one large roach every 2–3 weeks
Do not handle: fast, defensive (slaps the ground and bites) and has medically significant venom
warn: Advanced species: defensive with medically significant venom. Do not handle.

sources.name: The Tarantula Collective – Cyriopagopus lividus care guide

ta-theraphosa-stirmi.title: Burgundy Goliath Birdeater Tarantula
ta-theraphosa-stirmi.summary: One of the giant Goliath birdeaters, from humid forest in Guyana and Brazil. It's a huge, heavy display spider with a deep burrowing habit and some of the most irritating defensive hairs of any tarantula, so it's not for handling.
rows: Leg span about 10–11 in (25–28 cm); body about 4–4.7 in
Females 12–20+ years; males much shorter after maturing
One per enclosure. Adults: at least 18 × 12 × 12 in (45 × 30 × 30 cm); 24 × 18 × 18 in with deep substrate is better. Heavy and tip-proof, with a low fall height
Deep, damp lower substrate with a retreat to burrow
75–85% with a deep damp lower layer and good ventilation
Large roaches, crickets, locusts and occasional worms; no need for vertebrate prey. Wait until fangs are fully black after a molt (a week or more for adults)
Do not handle: very irritating hairs (dangerous to eyes and airways) and a venomous bite. Wear gloves and eye protection for rehousing
notes: Often confused with T. blondi in the trade.
warn: Advanced species: severe urticating hairs and a venomous bite. Do not handle.

sources.name: Herpeton Academy – Theraphosa stirmi care guide

ta-heteroscodra-maculata.title: Ornamental Baboon (Togo Starburst) Tarantula
ta-heteroscodra-maculata.summary: A chalky-white tarantula with black-and-brown mottling and thick back legs, from West Africa. It's a very fast, defensive tree-dwelling Old World species that lives in a webbed retreat, a display animal for experienced keepers only.
rows: Leg span about 5–6 in (12–15 cm); body about 2–2.4 in
Females often 10–12 years; males much shorter
One per enclosure. Adults: at least 8 × 8 × 12 in (20 × 20 × 30 cm, taller than wide) built around a firmly anchored vertical cork tube or bark slab
About 75–82°F (24–28°C) by day; a slight night drop is fine
Moderate to fairly high, but always with good ventilation; lightly moisten part of the substrate near the retreat
Crickets, roaches, locusts and similar insects; remove uneaten prey
Do not handle: extremely fast and defensive, and its venomous bite can cause pain, swelling, cramps and nausea
Arboreal; webs heavily around its retreat
Reaches full size in about 3 years
West Africa (Ghana, Togo and Benin region)
warn: Expert species: very fast, defensive and venomous. Plan every opening of the enclosure.

sources.name: Herpeton Academy – Heteroscodra maculata care guide

ta-pamphobeteus-sp-machala.title: Purple Starburst Birdeater Tarantula
ta-pamphobeteus-sp-machala.summary: A large, fast-growing ground tarantula from Ecuador, prized for the blue-violet sheen of mature males. It eats eagerly and grows quickly, has irritating defensive hairs, and is a display spider for confident keepers, not a handling pet.
rows: Leg span up to about 7–8.5 in (18–22 cm)
Large, low adult enclosure about 18 × 12 in (45 × 30 cm) floor with little open height
About 5–7 in (12–18 cm) of firm, compactable substrate and a broad retreat
About 72–81°F (22–27°C) by day, 68–73°F at night; no heat lamps or sunny windows
65–80% with a damp corner or lower layer and strong ventilation
Strong feeder; feed by body condition to avoid obesity, and remove prey before a molt
Not for handling: urticating hairs and a venomous bite; use gloves and eye protection for rehousing

sources.name: Herpeton Academy – Pamphobeteus sp. Machala care guide
